**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Status: Recommendation attached — decision requested by end of month**

Over the past six weeks we've looked closely at how our inference hardware is actually being used, and the picture is more complicated than our dashboards suggested. I want to lay out the trade-offs as we see them and make a recommendation, with the caveats attached.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward on its face. Our p99 latency has crept from 400ms to nearly 900ms during peak hours, and two of our internal customers have started building retry logic and caching layers to compensate — which is itself a form of hidden cost, since it adds complexity and masks the underlying problem. When latency degrades, people notice, and the people who notice are the ones whose goodwill keeps our platform funded. There's also a reliability argument: we're running close enough to the ceiling that a single hardware failure or a sustained traffic spike would force us to shed load. We've never had a formal incident from this, but we've come closer than any of us would like.

The case against buying is equally straightforward: the money, and what else it could do. A modest expansion — two additional nodes plus the networking and power work that entails — would consume most of our discretionary infrastructure budget for the year. That budget is also the most plausible funding source for the evaluation pipeline work, the observability overhaul, and the on-call tooling that the SRE team has been asking for since spring. Opportunity cost is easy to wave at and hard to quantify, but it's real. And hardware purchases are not meaningfully reversible. Once we've committed, the depreciation clock starts, and if our traffic mix changes — say, if the batch workloads migrate to the shared cluster as planned — we could find ourselves owning capacity we can't return and can't easily repurpose.

Which brings me to utilisation. Our average GPU utilisation sits around 38%, which sounds alarming until you unpack it. A meaningful fraction of that gap is structural: models pinned to specific nodes for latency reasons, batch jobs scheduled conservatively, and a queueing policy written eighteen months ago when our workload looked different. We believe — and this is the part where I want to flag genuine uncertainty — that better scheduling, dynamic batching, and a proper tiering of latency-sensitive versus throughput workloads could get us to 55–60% effective utilisation without new hardware. That would absorb our projected growth for roughly two quarters and, importantly, would cut p99 latency *today*, because most of our tail latency comes from contention, not raw capacity.

The uncertainty matters. Our estimate rests on profiling data from a three-week window that included an unusual traffic pattern, and the engineering effort to implement the scheduler changes is nontrivial — roughly six engineer-weeks, which is its own opportunity cost. There's also a risk that we optimise hard, discover the ceiling is real, and end up buying hardware later at a worse moment, having spent the intervening time on work that only deferred the problem. I don't think that risk is large, but I can't rule it out.

My recommendation is that we invest in utilisation first, with a defined trigger for hardware purchase. Concretely: fund the scheduling and batching work now, set a target of 55% effective utilisation and a p99 under 500ms, and pre-approve the hardware purchase to execute automatically if we hit either target and still project capacity shortfall within one quarter, or if we miss the targets by a meaningful margin after honest effort. This sequencing preserves optionality. The scheduler work is valuable regardless of what we eventually buy — better utilisation makes any future hardware go further — whereas hardware bought now is sunk cost if our utilisation hypothesis holds. The reversibility asymmetry alone justifies the ordering, even setting aside the budget question.

I want to be clear about what I'm *not* arguing. I'm not saying we should never buy hardware, or that the reliability concerns are imaginary. If we had a hard contractual latency SLA with external customers, I would probably recommend buying now and optimising later, because the downside of a visible failure would outweigh the savings. We don't have that — yet. But we should treat the current headroom as borrowed time and put the trigger conditions in writing so that "buy more" doesn't become a decision we keep deferring because the optimisation work is going well.

Happy to walk through the profiling data with anyone who wants the detail. I'd suggest we aim for a decision at the next leadership sync so the scheduling work can start before the quarter closes.
